aeo.what_is: PTSD develops after trauma, causing intrusive memories, avoidance, mood changes, and heightened arousal lasting over one month.

content.description: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a mental health condition that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. It is characterized by intrusive memories, avoidance of trauma reminders, negative changes in cognition and mood, and increased arousal. Symptoms persist for more than one month and cause significant distress or impairment.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A veteran flinches at fireworks and avoids July 4th celebrations entirely, staying home with curtains drawn.
An assault survivor changes their entire routine, taking different routes and avoiding places that remind them of the attack.
A car accident victim grips the door handle every time they're a passenger, scanning constantly for potential collisions.
A natural disaster survivor panics during rainstorms, reliving the flood that destroyed their home years ago.
A first responder wakes up screaming from nightmares about scenes they witnessed, unable to return to sleep.
A childhood abuse survivor feels detached from loved ones, struggling to feel joy even during happy moments.
A mass shooting witness avoids crowded places and experiences panic when hearing loud noises in public spaces.
A medical trauma survivor becomes hypervigilant in hospitals, experiencing flashbacks to their life-threatening illness.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief at finally understanding why they've been struggling and that their symptoms have a name.
Fear that they're permanently broken or will never feel normal again.
Shame about needing help or not being strong enough to overcome trauma alone.
Anger that one event could have such a lasting impact on their life.
Hope that treatment might reduce the intensity of intrusive memories and hypervigilance.
Concern about stigma, especially in military, first responder, or high-performance careers.
Validation that their suffering is real and recognized by the medical community.
Anxiety about having to revisit traumatic memories during treatment.

first_person_statements: I feel like I'm always waiting for the next terrible thing to happen, like my body won't let me relax even when I'm safe.
Sometimes I'm back there in that moment, and it feels just as real as the first time it happened.
I've become a completely different person since it happened—I don't recognize myself anymore.
People say I should just move on, but they don't understand that my brain won't let me forget.
I avoid so many things now that my world has become incredibly small, but facing reminders feels impossible.
The worst part isn't the nightmares—it's feeling disconnected from everyone I love, like I'm watching my life from behind glass.

content.temporal_criteria: Symptoms must persist for more than one month after the traumatic event. Acute stress reactions occurring within the first month may be diagnosed as Acute Stress Disorder. PTSD with delayed expression specifies when full diagnostic criteria are not met until at least 6 months after the trauma, though some symptoms may appear earlier.

misdiagnosis_explained.reason: Both involve hypervigilance and anxiety, but PTSD symptoms are linked to a specific trauma and include intrusive re-experiencing.
misdiagnosis_explained.key_difference: PTSD has identifiable trauma triggers and flashbacks; GAD features pervasive worry without trauma-specific content.

misdiagnosis_explained.reason: PTSD often includes mood symptoms like emotional numbing, loss of interest, and negative beliefs that overlap with depression.
misdiagnosis_explained.key_difference: PTSD includes trauma-related intrusion symptoms and hyperarousal, while pure depression lacks flashbacks and trauma-specific avoidance.

misdiagnosis_explained.reason: Both can involve intense fear reactions, physical arousal symptoms, and avoidance behaviors.
misdiagnosis_explained.key_difference: Panic attacks in PTSD are typically triggered by trauma reminders, while panic disorder involves unexpected attacks or fear of the attacks themselves.

misdiagnosis_explained.reason: Symptoms are nearly identical, making timing the critical distinction.
misdiagnosis_explained.key_difference: ASD occurs within 3 days to 1 month post-trauma; PTSD is diagnosed when symptoms persist beyond one month.

misdiagnosis_explained.reason: Both involve stress reactions to life events with mood and anxiety symptoms.
misdiagnosis_explained.key_difference: Adjustment disorder involves stressors that don't meet trauma criteria and lacks the specific symptom clusters of intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions, and arousal changes required for PTSD.

misdiagnosis_explained.reason: Both may involve emotional dysregulation, relationship difficulties, and dissociation, especially in complex trauma cases.
misdiagnosis_explained.key_difference: BPD features long-standing identity disturbance, fear of abandonment, and impulsivity as core features; PTSD has a clear trauma onset and specific re-experiencing symptoms.

real_life_examples.title: The Combat Veteran Who Couldn't Come Home
real_life_examples.baseline: Marcus, a 28-year-old former Marine, completed two tours in Afghanistan with distinction. Before deployment, he was outgoing, enjoyed socializing with friends, and planned to use his GI Bill to become a teacher.
real_life_examples.first_change: Three months after returning home, Marcus's girlfriend noticed he was sleeping only 2-3 hours per night, waking up drenched in sweat. He startled violently at car backfires and became irritable when she asked about his time overseas.
real_life_examples.behaviors: Marcus stopped attending family gatherings because crowds made him anxious. He obsessively checked door locks and windows multiple times nightly. He began drinking heavily to fall asleep and avoided driving on highways. He abandoned his teaching plans because he couldn't concentrate long enough to complete applications.
real_life_examples.consequences: His relationship ended after he lashed out during an argument, frightening his girlfriend. He lost his warehouse job after confronting a coworker he perceived as threatening. Friends stopped inviting him out after he repeatedly declined. He felt increasingly isolated and ashamed.
real_life_examples.aftermath: Marcus continues to struggle with intrusive memories of combat situations, avoids situations that remind him of his service, and feels emotionally numb around people he used to care about. His life has contracted significantly as avoidance behaviors expanded.

real_life_examples.title: The Accident That Rewired Everything
real_life_examples.baseline: Sophia, a 35-year-old marketing director, was driving home from work when a truck ran a red light and T-boned her car. Though she escaped with minor injuries, the other driver was severely hurt. Before the accident, Sophia was an independent, confident professional who loved road trips.
real_life_examples.first_change: Two months after the accident, Sophia still couldn't drive without experiencing full-body panic. She began having vivid nightmares about the collision, often waking up feeling like she was trapped in the car.
real_life_examples.behaviors: She started taking taxis everywhere despite the expense, maxing out credit cards. She avoided the intersection where the accident occurred, adding 30 minutes to any commute. She replayed the accident constantly, questioning whether she could have prevented it. She stopped visiting friends outside her neighborhood.
real_life_examples.consequences: Her work performance declined as she missed client meetings she couldn't reach by taxi. Colleagues noticed her jumpiness and inability to focus. She withdrew from her partner emotionally, feeling guilty for surviving relatively unharmed while the other driver suffered.
real_life_examples.aftermath: Sophia remains unable to drive and experiences intense physiological reactions to traffic sounds. She feels detached from her previous life and beliefs about safety, constantly anticipating danger. Her world has become geographically limited to taxi-accessible areas.

real_life_examples.title: The Assault That Shattered Trust
real_life_examples.baseline: Jennifer, a 22-year-old college senior, was assaulted by an acquaintance at a party. Previously outgoing and active in campus organizations, she had a close friend group and was planning graduate school applications.
real_life_examples.first_change: Within weeks of the assault, Jennifer stopped attending classes regularly. She experienced intrusive memories of the attack throughout the day, triggered by seemingly random things—a cologne scent, certain songs, the layout of rooms.
real_life_examples.behaviors: She avoided the building where the party occurred and eventually most of campus. She screened all calls and texts obsessively, fearing contact from the perpetrator. She slept in her closet because her bed felt exposed. She stopped going out at night entirely and dropped out of all social activities.
real_life_examples.consequences: Her grades plummeted, jeopardizing graduation. Friends felt shut out and gradually stopped reaching out. She missed graduate school deadlines. She felt intense shame and blamed herself for attending the party, beliefs that contradicted her rational understanding that assault is never the victim's fault.
real_life_examples.aftermath: Jennifer continues to experience flashbacks, especially in social situations or around men of similar appearance to her attacker. She struggles with persistent feelings of guilt and shame, difficulty trusting others, and emotional numbness that prevents her from feeling close to anyone.

real_life_examples.title: The First Responder Who Saw Too Much
real_life_examples.baseline: David, a 42-year-old paramedic with 15 years of experience, prided himself on staying calm in emergencies. He was married with two young children and coached his daughter's soccer team. He'd responded to countless traumatic calls throughout his career.
real_life_examples.first_change: After responding to a mass casualty event where multiple children died, David began experiencing unwanted images of the scene intruding into his thoughts constantly. He couldn't play with his own children without visualizing them injured.
real_life_examples.behaviors: He became emotionally detached from his family, going through motions but feeling nothing. He snapped at his wife over minor issues and withdrew to the garage for hours. He returned to work but felt overwhelming dread before each shift. He began drinking after shifts to quiet his mind.
real_life_examples.consequences: His work partner noticed delayed reaction times and uncharacteristic errors in judgment. His wife felt like she was living with a stranger. He stopped coaching soccer, unable to be around children without intrusive thoughts. He felt profound guilt that this event affected him when he'd handled so many others.
real_life_examples.aftermath: David continues to experience intrusive memories, emotional numbness toward his family, hypervigilance on calls, and persistent negative beliefs that he should have been able to save more people. His identity as a competent, calm professional feels shattered.

real_life_examples.title: The Survivor Who Lost Her Foundation
real_life_examples.baseline: Maria, a 50-year-old office manager, lived in the same coastal home for 20 years. She was organized, valued her routines, and felt deeply connected to her community. She'd weathered previous storms without major issues.
real_life_examples.first_change: After surviving a Category 5 hurricane that destroyed her home and killed several neighbors, Maria was relocated to temporary housing. She began having vivid nightmares of water rising and became unable to sleep when it rained.
real_life_examples.behaviors: She checked weather forecasts obsessively multiple times per hour. She couldn't make decisions about rebuilding, becoming paralyzed when faced with choices. She avoided news coverage of weather events and muted conversations about the hurricane. She hoarded water and supplies in her temporary apartment.
real_life_examples.consequences: She took leave from work, unable to concentrate or function in the office. She isolated from neighbors who wanted to discuss rebuilding plans. Simple decisions like where to buy groceries became overwhelming. She felt her sense of safety and control was permanently destroyed.
real_life_examples.aftermath: Maria experiences intense physiological reactions to rain and weather alerts, persistent feelings that another disaster is imminent, and inability to feel settled anywhere. She's lost her sense of the world as a predictable place and struggles to imagine a future that feels stable.

similarities: Both involve intrusion, avoidance, negative mood, and arousal symptoms following trauma.
Both require exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence.
Both cause significant distress and functional impairment.
differences: ASD occurs within 3 days to 1 month after trauma; PTSD persists beyond one month.
ASD diagnosis emphasizes dissociative symptoms more prominently than PTSD.
PTSD requires symptoms in all four clusters; ASD has more flexible criteria.
comparisons.clinical_note: If symptoms meeting PTSD criteria appear within the first month, clinicians should diagnose ASD initially and reassess at one month to determine if PTSD diagnosis is warranted.

similarities: Both involve psychological responses to stressful events.
Both can include anxiety and depressive symptoms.
Both may involve behavioral changes and functional impairment.
differences: PTSD requires exposure to trauma meeting specific criteria (death, serious injury, sexual violence); adjustment disorder involves stressors that don't meet trauma criteria.
PTSD has specific symptom clusters (intrusion, avoidance, cognitive/mood changes, arousal); adjustment disorder has more general emotional or behavioral symptoms.
PTSD symptoms must persist beyond one month; adjustment disorder is diagnosed when symptoms exceed what's expected but may resolve within 6 months of stressor ending.
comparisons.clinical_note: A person experiencing distress after job loss or divorce would receive an adjustment disorder diagnosis, while someone with persistent intrusive memories after witnessing a violent death would be evaluated for PTSD.

similarities: Both involve persistent anxiety and worry.
Both may include concentration difficulties, sleep problems, and irritability.
Both can cause significant impairment in daily functioning.
differences: PTSD anxiety is linked to a specific trauma and includes re-experiencing symptoms; GAD involves excessive worry about various everyday concerns without trauma focus.
PTSD includes avoidance of trauma-specific reminders; GAD doesn't have trauma-related avoidance.
PTSD features intrusive memories, flashbacks, and trauma-related nightmares; GAD doesn't involve re-experiencing a specific event.
comparisons.clinical_note: Hypervigilance in PTSD is typically focused on preventing trauma recurrence, while GAD worry is more diffuse and can shift between multiple concerns unrelated to trauma.

similarities: Both can involve persistent low mood, anhedonia, and emotional numbness.
Both may include social withdrawal and concentration difficulties.
Both can feature negative thoughts about self and future.
differences: PTSD includes trauma-specific intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares); MDD doesn't involve re-experiencing.
PTSD features hyperarousal and exaggerated startle response; these aren't core features of MDD.
PTSD negative cognitions are often trauma-related (guilt about surviving, persistent blame); MDD thoughts are more generally negative about self-worth.
comparisons.clinical_note: PTSD and MDD frequently co-occur. Thorough trauma history is essential because treating PTSD with trauma-focused therapy can also improve comorbid depressive symptoms.

faqs.question: Does everyone who experiences trauma develop PTSD?
faqs.answer: No, most people who experience trauma don't develop PTSD. Lifetime prevalence is around 6-8%, meaning the majority of trauma survivors are resilient and don't meet full diagnostic criteria. Factors like social support, coping skills, trauma severity, and prior mental health influence who develops PTSD.

faqs.question: Can PTSD develop years after a traumatic event?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is called PTSD with delayed expression. Some people don't meet full diagnostic criteria until at least 6 months after the trauma, though they may have had some symptoms earlier. Changes in life circumstances or new reminders can trigger symptom onset years later.

faqs.question: Is PTSD only diagnosed in combat veterans?
faqs.answer: No, PTSD can develop after any qualifying trauma including assault, accidents, natural disasters, medical trauma, witnessing violence, or learning about trauma to loved ones. While veterans have higher rates, anyone exposed to qualifying trauma can develop PTSD.

faqs.question: What's the difference between PTSD and remembering something traumatic?
faqs.answer: Everyone remembers traumatic events, but PTSD involves involuntary, intrusive re-experiencing that feels like the trauma is happening again, along with avoidance, negative thought changes, and hyperarousal. These symptoms persist for over a month and significantly impair functioning, going beyond normal memory.

faqs.question: Can PTSD go away on its own without treatment?
faqs.answer: Some people recover naturally with time and support, but many don't. Without treatment, PTSD often becomes chronic and may worsen. Early intervention improves outcomes. Evidence-based treatments like trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, and medications significantly improve symptoms for most people.

faqs.question: Will I have to relive my trauma in detail during treatment?
faqs.answer: Trauma-focused treatments involve processing the traumatic memory, but therapists use structured, gradual approaches to make this tolerable. You work with your therapist to face trauma memories at a pace you can manage. Avoidance maintains PTSD, so processing trauma, while difficult, is key to recovery.

faqs.question: What does a PTSD flashback actually feel like?
faqs.answer: Flashbacks involve suddenly feeling like the trauma is happening in the present moment. This can include vivid sensory experiences—seeing, hearing, or smelling aspects of the trauma. Some people lose awareness of their current surroundings completely, while others maintain some awareness but experience intense re-experiencing.

faqs.question: Can children develop PTSD?
faqs.answer: Yes, PTSD occurs across all ages, including young children. Symptoms may look different—young children might reenact trauma through play, have nightmares without clear content, or show regressive behaviors like bedwetting. Diagnostic criteria have some developmental modifications for children.

faqs.question: Why do I feel guilty about surviving when others didn't?
faqs.answer: Survivor guilt is a common PTSD symptom, particularly when others died or were seriously harmed in the same trauma. This involves persistent, distorted thoughts about personal responsibility. Cognitive processing therapy specifically addresses these guilt-related cognitions, which maintain PTSD symptoms.

faqs.question: Is PTSD the same thing as being traumatized?
faqs.answer: No. Being traumatized means experiencing a traumatic event and its immediate aftermath. PTSD is a specific diagnosis requiring particular symptoms across four categories that persist beyond one month and cause significant impairment. Many traumatized people don't develop PTSD.

faqs.question: Can PTSD symptoms get worse over time even if the trauma happened years ago?
faqs.answer: Yes, untreated PTSD can worsen over time. Avoidance behaviors often expand, shrinking a person's world. Additional stressors or new traumas can exacerbate symptoms. Anniversary reactions or new trauma reminders can intensify symptoms even years later. This is why treatment shouldn't be delayed.

faqs.question: Why am I emotionally numb instead of just anxious?
faqs.answer: Emotional numbing is a core PTSD symptom involving diminished interest in activities, detachment from others, and inability to experience positive emotions. This develops as the brain's way of managing overwhelming emotion but becomes problematic, preventing connection and joy. Trauma-focused treatment addresses numbing along with hyperarousal.

faqs.question: Do medications cure PTSD or just mask symptoms?
faqs.answer: SSRIs like sertraline and paroxetine don't just mask symptoms—they can reduce PTSD symptom severity by addressing underlying neurobiological changes. However, they work best combined with trauma-focused psychotherapy. Medications alone typically don't lead to full recovery, but they can make it easier to engage in effective therapy.

faqs.question: Why do I avoid things that logically I know are safe?
faqs.answer: Trauma changes the brain's threat detection system. The amygdala becomes hyperresponsive, flagging trauma reminders as dangerous even when rational thought says they're safe. Avoidance reduces short-term distress but maintains PTSD long-term. Treatment helps recalibrate threat detection through safe exposure to reminders.

faqs.question: What's the difference between PTSD and Complex PTSD?
faqs.answer: Complex PTSD, recognized in ICD-11 but not DSM-5, results from chronic or repeated trauma like long-term abuse. It includes PTSD symptoms plus disturbances in self-organization: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and relationship difficulties. Treatment requires addressing both PTSD symptoms and these additional challenges.

faqs.question: Can you have PTSD from emotional or psychological trauma without physical danger?
faqs.answer: DSM-5 criteria require exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. Purely emotional trauma without these elements wouldn't meet PTSD criteria, though it could cause other conditions like adjustment disorder. However, psychological abuse often co-occurs with threats that do meet criteria.

faqs.question: Why do I startle so easily now?
faqs.answer: Exaggerated startle response is a PTSD hyperarousal symptom. Trauma dysregulates the nervous system, leaving it in a state of high alert. Your body reacts to sudden stimuli as potential threats. This physiological change reflects altered brain functioning, particularly in the amygdala and stress response systems.

faqs.question: Is it normal to have PTSD symptoms that come and go?
faqs.answer: Yes, PTSD symptoms can fluctuate in intensity. Stressors, trauma reminders, anniversaries, or life changes can temporarily worsen symptoms. Some people experience periods of relative stability interrupted by symptom increases. This doesn't mean treatment isn't working—learning to manage fluctuations is part of recovery.

faqs.question: Can you develop PTSD from learning about trauma that happened to someone else?
faqs.answer: Yes, DSM-5 criteria include learning about trauma (involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence) to a close family member or friend. This is particularly relevant for family members of trauma victims. Additionally, repeated exposure to trauma details is included, relevant for professionals like first responders.

faqs.question: How is PTSD different from just being stressed or anxious about something bad that happened?
faqs.answer: PTSD involves specific symptom clusters—involuntary re-experiencing, effortful avoidance, negative cognitive and mood changes, and altered arousal—that persist beyond one month and significantly impair functioning. Normal stress responses don't include flashbacks, don't last as long, and don't cause the same level of impairment.

acute_stress_disorder.description: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) shares many symptoms with PTSD but occurs within 3 days to 1 month of trauma exposure. It includes intrusion, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal symptoms. If symptoms last beyond one month, PTSD may be diagnosed.
acute_stress_disorder.importance: Identifying ASD early allows for timely interventions that may reduce progression to PTSD.

complex_ptsd.description: Complex PTSD, recognized in ICD-11 but not in DSM-5, results from chronic or repeated trauma (e.g., long-term abuse, captivity). It includes PTSD symptoms plus disturbances in self-organization such as affect dysregulation, persistent negative self-concept, and difficulties in relationships.
complex_ptsd.note: Some individuals diagnosed with PTSD in DSM-5 may meet ICD-11 criteria for Complex PTSD, which can inform treatment planning.

mechanisms: Hyperactive amygdala leading to heightened fear and threat perception.
Reduced prefrontal cortex regulation over emotional responses.
Hippocampal volume reduction impairing memory contextualization.
Altered hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function affecting stress hormone release.

content.diagnostic_criteria: Exposure to trauma via direct experience, witnessing, learning about events to close others, or repeated exposure to aversive details. Symptoms include intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition/mood, and changes in arousal/reactivity, persisting more than one month and causing significant distress/impairment.
content.prevalence: Lifetime prevalence around 6–8% in the general population, higher in high-risk groups (combat veterans, assault survivors).
content.age_of_onset: Can occur at any age; higher risk in adolescence and early adulthood after trauma.
content.prognosis: Early treatment and social support improve outcomes; untreated PTSD can become chronic and debilitating.

history: Detailed trauma history, including type, timing, and severity.
Symptom onset, duration, and functional impact.
medical_workup: Rule out neurological injury or medical causes of symptoms.

intrusion: Recurrent, intrusive memories of the trauma.
Strong distress or physical reactions to trauma cues.
avoidance: Avoiding thoughts, feelings, or conversations about the trauma.
Avoiding places, people, or activities related to the trauma.
negative_alterations_in_cognition_and_mo: Persistent negative beliefs about oneself or the world.
Distorted self-blame or blame of others.
Persistent negative emotions such as fear, guilt, or shame.
Feeling detached or estranged from others.

biological: Genetic vulnerability to anxiety or mood disorders.
Female sex (higher risk in epidemiological studies).

impact_on_life.school_work: Reduced performance, concentration issues, and absenteeism.
impact_on_life.social: Avoidance of gatherings, social withdrawal, and relationship strain.
impact_on_life.medical: Increased risk of substance abuse, cardiovascular problems, and chronic pain.

medications: SSRIs such as sertraline and paroxetine.
care_coordination: Involving family or trusted supports when appropriate.
Coordination between mental health and primary care providers.

treatment_goals: Restore functioning and quality of life.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Attributing symptoms to depression or generalized anxiety without exploring trauma history.
Underreporting due to stigma or avoidance.
overdiagnosis_factors: Diagnosing PTSD for normal acute stress reactions before one month has passed.

specifiers.with_delayed_expression: Onset of full criteria at least 6 months after the event.

adults: Emotional numbing, strained relationships, reduced work performance.
